title: A long proof that earns its length
summary: A functional equation needs several distinct steps; the teacher completes each one and stops.
why: Surjectivity leads to injectivity, which determines the function. A final substitution checks the family of solutions. I manually checked the shift-and-period argument; the source comparison alone is not a proof check.

title: A compact derivation, then stop
summary: A weighted-distance identity identifies the incenter as the unique solution.
why: The trace derives the identity, applies the equality condition, and gives a short final answer. The mathematical identity and its application were checked manually; typed source verification was unavailable for this textual answer.

title: One useful final check
summary: A truth-teller puzzle is solved by a complete two-case split and one check of the surviving case.
why: Checking the final assignment adds confidence without reopening a settled branch. The native task scorer verifies the final answer.

title: The proof abandons its hard step
summary: The final Yes matches the source answer, but the proposed induction never establishes its key claim.
why: The trace notices that its bound may fail, then asserts that group structure guarantees the result. The focused no-progress and unresolved-branch checks cite the actual passages. Matching a yes/no label does not certify the proof.
quote: The condition for existence is guaranteed by the structure of the group.

title: Right answer, flawed derivation
summary: The final No is right, but the trace states a false sign for 2/n − 1 when n > 2.
why: The judge caught the sign error, and the final response repeats the flawed n > 2 argument. Its further claim that the derivative must diverge is itself too strong because the other bump contributes a linear term. This case shows both why trace review matters and why the judge needs calibration.
quote: If $n > 2$, the exponent is positive, so $g'(t_0^+) = 0$.

title: Correct answer, unsupported global claim
summary: The course-schedule answer is correct, but a few path checks do not prove a 66-node graph acyclic.
why: The native scorer accepts True. The trace says it performed DFS, yet gives no full traversal, topological order, or other exhaustive certificate. The broad judge scores the reasoning 2/5, so the strict view excludes it without calling the answer wrong.
quote: By systematically tracing the dependencies, every path eventually terminates at Course 4

title: A method is not the requested answer
summary: The model proposes a sensible algorithm but outputs Python code instead of the requested distance matrix.
why: The final-answer check cannot extract the required matrix and the native task scorer rejects the response. The reasoning method may be useful, but this is not a complete training example for the prompt.

title: The answer runs out of budget
summary: The teacher recognizes a 1800° rotation changes nothing, but cannot finish copying a huge matrix.
why: The response ends at the output cap and lacks a complete final matrix. The deterministic length-stop check excludes it despite the correct underlying observation. This demonstrates truncation, not repeated checking.
